content: The provision of vaccines during the training of healthcare professionals, prior to any potential blood exposure, can both increase vaccination rates among personnel and prevent infections in trainees who are at heightened risk of accidental injuries while learning medical techniques. Pre-vaccination serologic screening for susceptibility to hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is not generally recommended for individuals being vaccinated unless the healthcare organization deems such screening to be cost-effective. Post-vaccination screening for antibodies to hepatitis B surface antigen (anti-HBs) is advised for personnel at ongoing risk of blood exposure to confirm vaccine response and to guide decisions regarding post-exposure prophylaxis or the need for revaccination. Healthcare personnel who fail to respond to or do not complete the primary vaccination series should either be revaccinated with a second three-dose vaccine series or evaluated to determine if they are hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) seropositive. Individuals who are revaccinated should be tested for anti-HBs at the completion of the second vaccine series. If they still do not respond, no further vaccination series should be administered, and they should be evaluated for the presence of HBsAg, which may indicate chronic HBV infection. No specific work restrictions are recommended for non-responders; however, in the event of percutaneous exposure to blood or body fluids, they should consult their healthcare providers promptly to assess the need for post-exposure prophylaxis. Personnel in chronic dialysis centers who do not respond to the vaccine should be screened for HBsAg and anti-HBs every six months. Vaccine-induced antibodies decline gradually over time, and up to 60% of individuals who initially respond to vaccination may lose detectable anti-HBs within eight years. Booster doses of the vaccine are not routinely recommended, as individuals who respond to the initial vaccine series remain protected against clinical hepatitis and chronic infection even when their anti-HBs levels become low or undetectable. The need for post-exposure prophylaxis, vaccination, or both depends on the HBsAg status of the exposure source and the immunization status of the exposed individual. Vaccination should be offered after any exposure in an unvaccinated person. If the source is known to be HBsAg seropositive, hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) should be administered, preferably within 24 hours. The effectiveness of HBIG given more than seven days after HBV exposure is unknown. If the source is HBsAg seropositive and the exposed individual is known not to have responded to a three-dose vaccine series, a single dose of HBIG and a dose of hepatitis B vaccine should be administered as soon as possible, with subsequent vaccine doses given at one month and six months after the initial dose. If the exposed individual is known not to have responded to both a three-dose vaccine series and revaccination, two doses of HBIG should be administered—one dose as soon as possible after exposure and the second dose one month later. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is the primary cause of parenterally transmitted non-A, non-B hepatitis in the United States. Over the past decade, the annual number of newly acquired HCV infections has ranged from an estimated 180,000 in 1984 to 28,000 in 1995. Of these, an estimated 2% to 4% occurred among healthcare personnel who were occupationally exposed to blood. A case-control study conducted before the identification of HCV demonstrated a significant association between the acquisition of non-A, non-B hepatitis and healthcare employment, particularly in patient care or laboratory work. Seroprevalence studies among hospital-based healthcare personnel have shown anti-HCV seroprevalence rates ranging from 1% to 2%. A history of accidental needlesticks has been independently associated with anti-HCV seropositivity in healthcare personnel. Several case reports have documented the transmission of HCV infection from anti-HCV-seropositive patients to healthcare personnel as a result of accidental needlesticks or cuts with sharp instruments. The rate of HCV transmission in studies using HCV RNA polymerase chain reaction methods was approximately 10%. The incubation period for hepatitis C is six to seven weeks, and nearly all individuals with acute infection will develop chronic HCV infection, characterized by persistent viremia and the potential for transmission to others. Serologic assays to detect anti-HCV are commercially available, but their interpretation is limited by several factors: (a) approximately 5% of HCV-infected individuals will not have detectable anti-HCV; (b) these assays cannot distinguish between acute, chronic, and past infections; (c) there may be a prolonged interval between the onset of acute illness and seroconversion; and (d) in populations with a low prevalence of HCV infection, commercial screening assays for anti-HCV yield a high proportion (up to 50%) of false-positive results. Although no true confirmatory test exists, supplemental tests for specificity are available and should be used to validate repeatedly reactive results from screening assays. The effectiveness of immune globulin for post-exposure prophylaxis after occupational exposure to HCV has been difficult to assess, but post-exposure prophylaxis with immune globulin does not appear to prevent HCV infection. Current immune globulin preparations are manufactured from plasma that has been screened for HCV antibodies, and positive lots are excluded from use. An experimental study in chimpanzees found that administration of immune globulin manufactured from anti-HCV-screened plasma one hour after exposure to HCV did not prevent infection or disease.
